ch14_ex1_q1a: Memorise the core ladder: $30^\circ = \frac{\pi}{6}$, $45^\circ = \frac{\pi}{4}$, $60^\circ = \frac{\pi}{3}$, $90^\circ = \frac{\pi}{2}$. Almost every exact-value angle is a whole-number multiple of one of these.
ch14_ex1_q1b: Divide by 180 as a decimal: $\frac{144}{180} = 0.8 = \frac{4}{5}$, so the answer is $\frac{4\pi}{5}$.
Alternatively, $144^\circ = 4 \times 36^\circ$ and $36^\circ = \frac{\pi}{5}$ (a fifth of a half-turn).
ch14_ex1_q1c: Count steps of $60^\circ$: $240 = 4 \times 60$, so it is $4 \times \frac{\pi}{3}$.
Quadrant check: $240^\circ$ is in quadrant 3, so the answer must lie between $\pi$ and $\frac{3\pi}{2}$; $\frac{4}{3} \approx 1.33$ is between 1 and 1.5.
ch14_ex1_q1d: Count steps of $30^\circ$: $330 = 11 \times 30$, and each $30^\circ$ is $\frac{\pi}{6}$, giving $\frac{11\pi}{6}$ straight away.
ch14_ex1_q1e: $420^\circ = 360^\circ + 60^\circ$, so $\frac{7\pi}{3} = 2\pi + \frac{\pi}{3}$: it lands on exactly the same unit-circle point as $\frac{\pi}{3}$, so it has the same sine and cosine.
ch14_ex1_q1f: $480^\circ - 360^\circ = 120^\circ$, so $\frac{8\pi}{3}$ sits at the same point as $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ in quadrant 2.
ch14_ex1_q2a: Read $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ as $\pi - \frac{\pi}{3}$, i.e. $180^\circ - 60^\circ$. Seeing it as 'a half-turn minus a familiar angle' is exactly what you need later for exact values in quadrant 2.
ch14_ex1_q2b: $\frac{5\pi}{6} = \pi - \frac{\pi}{6}$: just $30^\circ$ short of a half-turn, so it is a quadrant 2 angle with reference angle $\frac{\pi}{6}$.
ch14_ex1_q2c: Quick quadrant read: with denominator 6, a numerator between 6 and 9 means the angle is between $\pi$ and $\frac{3\pi}{2}$, i.e. quadrant 3.
ch14_ex1_q2d: Think of $0.9\pi$ as $\pi - 0.1\pi$: that is $180^\circ - 18^\circ = 162^\circ$, an easy mental calculation.
ch14_ex1_q2e: Size check: $\frac{5}{9}$ is just over $\frac{1}{2}$, so the angle is just over half of $180^\circ$, i.e. a bit more than $90^\circ$. $100^\circ$ fits.
ch14_ex1_q2f: $\frac{9\pi}{5} = 2\pi - \frac{\pi}{5}$, so it is $360^\circ - 36^\circ = 324^\circ$, a quadrant 4 angle.
ch14_ex1_q2g: Split it: $\frac{11\pi}{9} = \pi + \frac{2\pi}{9} = 180^\circ + 40^\circ$, which also tells you it is in quadrant 3.
ch14_ex1_q2h: Use $2\pi - 0.2\pi$: $360^\circ - 36^\circ = 324^\circ$. Decimal multiples of $\pi$ often convert faster as 'distance from a full turn'.
ch14_ex1_q3a: Many calculators convert directly: in degree mode, enter the angle with the radian symbol (e.g. $0.6^{r}$) and it returns degrees.
ch14_ex1_q3b: Measure from $\frac{\pi}{2}$: $1.89 - 1.57 = 0.32$ rad $\approx 18^\circ$, so the angle is about $90^\circ + 18^\circ = 108^\circ$.
ch14_ex1_q3c: Measure back from $\pi$: $3.14 - 2.9 \approx 0.24$ rad $\approx 14^\circ$, so the angle is about $180^\circ - 14^\circ = 166^\circ$.
ch14_ex1_q3d: $4.31 - \pi \approx 1.17$ rad $\approx 67^\circ$, so the angle is about $180^\circ + 67^\circ = 247^\circ$, in quadrant 3.
ch14_ex1_q3e: $3.72 - 3.14 \approx 0.58$ rad $\approx 33^\circ$, so expect about $213^\circ$: just into quadrant 3.
ch14_ex1_q3f: Measure back from a full turn: $2\pi - 5.18 \approx 1.10$ rad $\approx 63^\circ$, so the angle is about $360^\circ - 63^\circ = 297^\circ$.
ch14_ex1_q3g: $\frac{3\pi}{2} \approx 4.712$, so $4.73$ rad is only just past $270^\circ$; an answer of about $271^\circ$ is exactly what you should expect.
ch14_ex1_q3h: $2\pi - 6 \approx 0.283$ rad, and $0.283 \times 57.3 \approx 16.2^\circ$, so the angle is about $360^\circ - 16.2^\circ \approx 343.8^\circ$.
ch14_ex1_q4c: $107^\circ = 90^\circ + 17^\circ$, so the answer is $1.571 + 0.297 \approx 1.87$. Compare with $73^\circ \approx 1.27$: they sit symmetrically either side of $\frac{\pi}{2}$.
ch14_ex1_q4e: Size check: $84.1^\circ$ is just under $90^\circ$, so the answer must be just under $\frac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.571$.
ch14_ex1_q4g: Anchor on a known angle: $135^\circ = \frac{3\pi}{4} \approx 2.356$, so $136.4^\circ$ should be just above that. $2.38$ fits.
ch14_ex1_q5a: $-\frac{\pi}{3}$ and $\frac{5\pi}{3}$ mark the same unit-circle point ($-60^\circ$ and $300^\circ$ differ by $360^\circ$), so they have identical sine and cosine.
ch14_ex1_q5b: $-4\pi$ is two complete clockwise revolutions, so it ends back at $(1, 0)$ and behaves exactly like an angle of 0.
ch14_ex1_q5c: $-3\pi$ is one and a half turns clockwise, ending at $(-1, 0)$: the same point as $\pi$.
ch14_ex1_q5d: A half-turn either way lands on $(-1, 0)$, so $-\pi$ and $\pi$ name the same point on the unit circle.
ch14_ex1_q5e: $\frac{5\pi}{3} = 2\pi - \frac{\pi}{3}$: a quadrant 4 angle with reference angle $\frac{\pi}{3}$, i.e. $360^\circ - 60^\circ$.
ch14_ex1_q5f: Add $2\pi$: $-\frac{11\pi}{6} + \frac{12\pi}{6} = \frac{\pi}{6}$, so $-330^\circ$ lands on the same point as $30^\circ$.
ch14_ex1_q5g: $\frac{23\pi}{6} = 4\pi - \frac{\pi}{6}$, so $690^\circ = 720^\circ - 30^\circ$: two full turns less $30^\circ$, landing in quadrant 4.
ch14_ex1_q5h: Add $4\pi$ ($= \frac{24\pi}{6}$): $-\frac{23\pi}{6} + \frac{24\pi}{6} = \frac{\pi}{6}$, so this angle sits at the same point as $30^\circ$.
ch14_ex1_q6a: Any whole number of revolutions, clockwise or anticlockwise, returns to $(1, 0)$, so $-2\pi$ gives the same sine and cosine as 0.
ch14_ex1_q6b: $-540^\circ = -360^\circ - 180^\circ$: one full clockwise turn then a half-turn, ending at $(-1, 0)$.
ch14_ex1_q6c: Add $360^\circ$: $-240^\circ + 360^\circ = 120^\circ$, so $-\frac{4\pi}{3}$ marks the same point as $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ in quadrant 2.
ch14_ex1_q6d: Quick method: divide by 180 to get the multiple of $\pi$ directly. $-720 \div 180 = -4$, i.e. two clockwise revolutions.
ch14_ex1_q6e: Add $360^\circ$: $-330^\circ + 360^\circ = 30^\circ$, so $-\frac{11\pi}{6}$ has the same sine and cosine as $\frac{\pi}{6}$.
ch14_ex1_q6f: Add $360^\circ$: $-210^\circ + 360^\circ = 150^\circ$, so $-\frac{7\pi}{6}$ marks the same point as $\frac{5\pi}{6}$ in quadrant 2.
ch14_ex1_q7a: All four points have $|x| = |y| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.71$; only the signs change. Each step of $\frac{\pi}{2}$ moves you to the next quadrant.
These points are where the circle meets the lines $y = x$ and $y = -x$, which is why $\tan$ is $\pm 1$ at each of them.
ch14_ex1_q7b: $\frac{\pi}{3}$ and $-\frac{\pi}{3}$ are mirror images in the $x$-axis: same $x$, opposite $y$. This is why $\cos(-t) = \cos t$ but $\sin(-t) = -\sin t$.
$\frac{2\pi}{3} = \pi - \frac{\pi}{3}$ is the mirror image of $\frac{\pi}{3}$ in the $y$-axis.
ch14_ex1_q7c: For the $\frac{\pi}{6}$ family the point is close to the $x$-axis, so the larger coordinate, $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, is the $x$-value and the smaller, $\frac{1}{2}$, is the $y$-value.
